title: Beauty is in the pie of the beholder
text:
Beauty is in the pie of the beholder
We asked readers to dish on their Thanksgiving favorites and created – what else? – pie charts to display the answers.
To keep peace, you might not want to raise this topic at the Thanksgiving dinner table.
No, not politics. Pie.
Americans have long debated which dessert goes best with our November harvest holiday. Pumpkin? Sweet potato? Apple?
To settle the age-old debate over which pie takes the holiday season, we asked our readers. Find a slice of our data, and see how your favorite pie compares.
We asked Monitor readers to settle this question once and for all. Some respondents brought lesser-known contestants to the stage. Cranberry pecan, mince, and even cranberry pudding pie got a slice of the spotlight. But pumpkin pie wears the crown among hundreds of polled readers.
Thanksgiving comes with plenty of traditions and lots of opinions. We asked about yours – including the controversial issue of when to put up Christmas decorations.
Here’s what you said:
Turkey stays king of the Thanksgiving table, according to our unscientific survey, with 66% of you saying it’s a must-have. But the bird wasn’t always the holiday’s undisputed centerpiece. Although wild “fowl” was served at the 1621 feast shared by the Wampanoag people and the pilgrim settlers of Plymouth colony, historians aren’t certain that turkey was on the menu. It wasn’t until the mid-19th century that the bird became associated with Thanksgiving.
Thanksgiving isn’t all about food, of course. Many Americans also enjoy watching football – a tradition that dates back to at least 1876 when Yale defeated Princeton (2-0) in a game on Thanksgiving Day. Then, the primary way to score points was to kick the ball between the goal posts. Touchdowns earned teams the right to attempt a kick for a “goal.” Professional football has held games on Thanksgiving Day since 1920.
But Monitor readers have their priorities straight. When it comes to the best part of Thanksgiving, a majority of Monitor readers who took the survey say it’s spending more time with family and friends.
And while stores may already be swapping out pumpkins for Christmas trees, not everyone is ready to move on to the next holiday. Sixty percent of respondents say Thanksgiving deserves at least a week to breathe before bringing out the jingle bells.
